summary: Tunisia lets citizens of a broad list of countries — every EU state except Cyprus, the UK, US, Canada, Japan, most of the rest of Europe, many Arab and African states and some Asian ones — enter visa-free for up to 90 days. Nationalities outside the list apply for a consular visa; Israeli passport holders are not admitted.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for the duration of your stay and in good condition: travellers who enter with a damaged or torn passport may have difficulty leaving.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Tunisia entry requirements

travelInsurance.text: No official source makes insurance a condition of entry for visa-exempt tourists. The UK government advises insurance for local treatment and medical evacuation: there is no free medical care for foreign nationals, and doctors' fees, medicines and private-clinic treatment must be paid on the spot.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Tunisia travel advice (health)

onwardTicket.text: Border officials have the right to ask for your onward or return ticket, proof of a hotel booking or other accommodation details, and your contact details. A small number of visitors have been refused entry or delayed for lack of evidence of accommodation.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Tunisia travel advice (entry requirements)

proofOfFunds.text: No official source we could read states a proof-of-funds requirement or amount for Tunisia. The UK Foreign Office says border officials may ask for your contact details, your onward or return travel tickets and proof of a hotel booking or other accommodation; it does not mention funds.

currencyLimits.text: Any import or export of foreign currency worth TND 20,000 or more must be declared to Customs on entry, on exit and in transit. A non-resident can take out more than TND 5,000 of the foreign banknotes they brought in only if they declared them on entry, and at most TND 30,000 (above that, through a bank); the declaration is valid for 3 months and one trip, and can be made online in advance. Tunisian dinars may not be taken out of the country, so keep exchange receipts to reconvert leftover dinars before you leave.

source.name: Douane tunisienne — Devises et change
source.instrument: Arrêté du Ministre des finances du 24 juillet 2019 (montants des articles 100, 107, 108, 114 et 140 de la loi n° 2015-26); avis de change du ministre des finances, JORT du 3 février 2006

notes: The UK FCDO says Tunisia has strict currency controls: check whether you must declare foreign currency on arrival (failure to declare may lead to confiscation), and keep declaration documents and official exchange receipts.
The UK FCDO says it is illegal to bring drones into Tunisia without authorisation; any drone detected will be confiscated and stored until your departure.

payments.text: The Government of Canada says many establishments in urban and tourist areas accept credit cards and ATMs are widely available in tourist areas and all major centres. Importing and exporting Tunisian dinars is prohibited, so you can only get dinars in Tunisia.

safety.text: The main tourist areas — Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse, Djerba — are generally safe with normal precautions. Governments advise against travel to the Libyan and Algerian border zones and the Chaambi mountain area, and a state of emergency remains formally in place.

bestTimeToVisit.text: No official seasonal guidance. The Government of Canada says northern summers are hot and dry and winters rainy (the rainy season generally runs from October to May in the north), and that from June to September temperatures can exceed 40°C with frequent sand and dust storms.

idp.text: Tunisia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Tunisia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Tunisia yet.

tips.text: The Government of Canada says importing and exporting Tunisian dinars is prohibited, so exchange money in Tunisia. The UK FCDO advises keeping official exchange receipts.

If you overstay your allowance without a valid reason you will be fined; the UK Foreign Office says you can pay on departure at the airport or in advance at some police stations. If you need longer than 90 days, ask a Tunisian embassy or consulate before you travel.

Avoid the immediate border areas with Libya and Algeria and the Chaambi mountain region — governments warn of terrorism and military operations there. The Sahara south of Remada is a designated military zone requiring authorization.
Carry proof of accommodation and a return or onward ticket — border officers may ask for them.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Tunisia?
faq.answer: Most Western tourists do not. Citizens of the EU (except Cyprus), UK, US, Canada, Japan, and much of the rest of Europe, the Arab world and Africa, as well as Argentina, Brazil and Chile, can stay visa-free for up to 90 days. Nationalities outside the exemption list — including most of South Asia and many African states — need a consular visa before travel.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Tunisia without a visa?
faq.answer: 90 days for most exempt nationalities (South Koreans get 30 days). For a longer stay, the Government of Canada advises contacting a Tunisian embassy or consulate before you leave. If you overstay without a valid reason you will be fined; the UK Foreign Office says you can pay on departure at the airport or in advance at some police stations.

faq.question: Can I bring Tunisian dinars in or out of the country?
faq.answer: No. The dinar is non-convertible and its import and export are prohibited. Exchange foreign currency inside Tunisia, keep the receipts, and reconvert leftover dinars before departure. Large amounts of foreign cash must be declared on arrival.

faq.question: Can Israeli citizens visit Tunisia?
faq.answer: No — Israeli passport holders are not admitted to Tunisia.

faq.question: Is Tunisia safe for tourists?
faq.answer: The coastal resorts and main cities are generally safe with normal precautions, and tourism infrastructure is well developed. Avoid the Libyan and Algerian border zones and the Chaambi mountains, which carry government travel warnings.

faq.question: Do I need a return ticket to enter Tunisia?
faq.answer: Formally entry is at the officer's discretion, but airlines and border police regularly ask visa-exempt visitors for a return or onward ticket and accommodation details. Carry both.
